name: Pedro Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Pedro. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, which is independent of companies, unions and parties. Nothing you say gets your name on it. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at five in the afternoon and finish around one in the morning, delivering takeaways on my 125 motorbike through FoodHop. Most nights it's 25 to 30 orders around the city centre and the student streets. On Sundays I do grocery parcels for the supermarket's home delivery app in their small vans, because that's steady money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's in your life, at home and at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented room above a launderette, £450 a month. I send my mum £100 a month because her back is bad and she can't work much. At work there's my friend Luis, who I've ridden with for five years, and we have the same coffee at the petrol station at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, people can stop talking about it. I'd tell Luis we were right not to panic. Then I'd go back to moaning about the potholes on Mill Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's okay, and FoodHop always has orders on weekend nights. My bike is paid off and my room is cheap, but a crash means no pay, and my mum's £100 a month goes first. I've only got maybe three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd try to keep £50 a month aside instead of spending it on the phone I don't need. I'd maybe use the AI thing on my phone to help me write a proper CV, because Luis did that and got an interview at the wholesaler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relaxed. A little thought in the back of my head about the money, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned crashing. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago a car pulled out on the ring road and I went over the bonnet. Bruised ribs, two weeks off, no pay. That's when I started sending less to my mum for a while, and I still feel bad about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Luis's interview at the wholesaler look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was for a van driver with a proper contract, delivering to shops and cafés. He didn't get it, but they said try again in spring. I'd think about it if he gets in and likes it.

say: People can **stop talking about AI**, and he'd tell Luis they were right.
He'd go back to complaining about the **potholes** on Mill Street.
think: His **paid-off bike** and cheap room make him feel mostly okay.
With about **three weeks** saved, a crash or breakdown would be tight.
do: Keep doing **FoodHop nights** and Sunday supermarket shifts.
Save **£50 a month** instead of buying a new phone.
Use an **AI app** to write a proper CV, like Luis did.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with a constant small **money worry**.
S0.quote: My bike is paid off and my room is cheap, but a crash means no pay, and my mum's £100 a month goes first.
fieldNote: Pedro feels fairly **secure** because his costs are low and his bike is owned.
His big fear is **injury**, after a crash two years ago cost him two weeks' pay.
He follows his friend Luis's moves, showing a **wait-for-proof** approach.

steps.text: Keep riding FoodHop nights and Sunday supermarket shifts
Put £50 a month aside instead of buying a new phone
Write a proper CV with an AI app on his phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the end of the world, people will adjust. Some jobs go, some come. I'd say that at the petrol station to Luis and anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd watch who starts riding. If people lose office jobs and sign up to FoodHop, then my weekend nights get split three ways. And the supermarket might use AI to plan the vans better and need fewer of us on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what really happens. If Luis gets the wholesaler job and says it's good, I'd apply too. I'd also cut my phone plan from £30 to £10 and try to build two months of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. Like waiting at a red light that's taking too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few months. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many orders I get on a Saturday compared to now, about 14. If my Saturday orders on FoodHop drop under 10, that's my sign. Numbers don't lie, people do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the AI planning the Sunday vans. Would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they give it to me, sure, I'll use it. I'm not against it, I just don't go looking. My phone already tells me where to go, so what's one more voice.

say: It's **not the end** of the world, and people will adjust.
Some jobs go and **some come**, he'd tell Luis at the petrol station.
think: Office workers joining FoodHop could **split his weekend** orders three ways.
AI van planning could mean **fewer Sunday shifts** at the supermarket.
do: **Wait a few months** and watch his Saturday order count.
Apply to the **wholesaler** if Luis gets in and likes it.
Cut his **phone plan** from £30 to £10 to build two months' savings.
feel: **Tense**, like a red light that's taking too long.
S1.quote: If my Saturday orders on FoodHop drop under 10, that's my sign. Numbers don't lie, people do.
fieldNote: Pedro sets a **clear trigger**: fewer than 10 Saturday orders means he moves.
He's pragmatic about AI tools: he'll use them if given, but **doesn't seek them**.
His mood shifts to **anxious** because both his income streams could shrink.

steps.text: Track Saturday FoodHop orders for a few months
Apply to the wholesaler van job if Luis recommends it
Cut the phone plan from £30 to £10 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's not lose our heads, but the government needs to have a plan quickly. I'm not for big promises, I'm for sensible stuff, like help with retraining. I'd probably say that in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the motorbike has about five years left in it. The thinking AI in 2028 doesn't take my delivery job, but the robots in 2031 do. I'd be 32 and need a trade that robots can't do well yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at an electrician apprenticeship straight away, because old houses with bad wiring seem like the last thing a robot will handle. It's three years, so I'd do it while still riding nights. I'd stop sending my mum money for a while, and that hurts to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pressure, a lot of pressure. But it's the kind where you know what to do, you just don't know if you'll make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you do an apprenticeship and ride nights at the same time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis says no, I'd fall asleep on the bike. Maybe weekends only, then. It'd mean £600 a month less, and I don't know how I'd cover that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your mum about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go see her in person, not on the phone. I'd tell her it's for two years, so in five years I can send her more. She'd say don't worry, and then she'd worry.

say: Don't **lose our heads**, but the government needs a plan quickly.
He backs **sensible help** like retraining, not big promises.
think: The motorbike job has about **five years** left before robots arrive around 2031.
At 32 he'll need **a trade** that robots can't do well yet.
do: Ride **weekend nights only** while training, losing about £600 a month.
Pause the **£100 a month** he sends his mum.
feel: Heavy **pressure**, with a plan but no certainty it will work.
S2.quote: The thinking AI in 2028 doesn't take my delivery job, but the robots in 2031 do. I'd be 32 and need a trade that robots can't do well yet.
fieldNote: Pedro uses the **three-year robot gap** to plan an electrician apprenticeship.
Stopping money to his mum is **the cost he hates** most.
He can't say how he'd cover **£600 a month** less while training.

steps.text: Apply for a three-year electrician apprenticeship
Cut FoodHop riding to weekend nights during training
Pause the £100 he sends his mum each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it properly. I'd say the same at the petrol station as in the fast one: sensible help, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years before AGI and eight before robots, I could do the apprenticeship without rushing. I'd still be riding till maybe 2030, then electrician work. I'd be about 35 when robots come for the motorbike deliveries, and I'd already be off the bike and wiring houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride full-time for one more year and save up, maybe £1,500, then start the apprenticeship. I'd keep sending mum her £100, just less often. And I'd use the AI on my phone to revise the maths, because I was bad at it at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Still tight on money, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You were bad at maths. Does that worry you about the electrician course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. But Luis's brother is an electrician and he says it's mostly Ohm's law and measuring. I'd practise on my phone on breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Luis doesn't do anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go anyway, it's my life. But I'd try to bring him along, because riding with someone for five years is like a brother. I'd keep nagging him at midnight coffee.

say: Five years is a **fair warning**, so people should use it properly.
He'd keep calling for **sensible help**, not panic.
think: He could do the **apprenticeship** without rushing and leave riding by about 2030.
When robots reach the bike around **2034**, he'd already be off it.
do: Ride full-time **one more year** to save about £1,500.
Start the **electrician apprenticeship** after that year.
Use an **AI tutor** on his phone to revise maths.
feel: **Better**, still tight on money but able to breathe.
S3.quote: I'd be about 35 when robots come for the motorbike deliveries, and I'd already be off the bike and wiring houses.
fieldNote: Five years lets Pedro **save first** and keep supporting his mum.
He plans to use **AI for maths** revision, a step up from his usual caution.
Loyalty to his friend Luis shapes his plans, but he'd **go alone** if needed.

steps.text: Ride FoodHop full-time one more year and save £1,500
Start an electrician apprenticeship after that year
Revise school maths with an AI tutor on his phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so no excuses for anyone. I'd say people should start planning, but not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to AGI and thirteen to robots means I could ride till maybe 2033. I'd still want a trade, though, because riding at 40 in the rain is not a life. This one doesn't scare me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for two years, then do the apprenticeship around 2029. I'd keep sending mum the full £100. I might move in with Luis to share rent, which would save us both £150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, apart from the usual money thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said riding at 40 is not a life. Would you leave even without robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. My knees already complain in the winter, so the robots just give me a date to get off the motorbike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you put it off too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfort. If FoodHop gets busy and the money's okay, I'd tell myself next year. My mum would push me, she always wanted me to have a trade.

say: There's **plenty of time**, so there are no excuses for anyone.
People should **start planning** now, he'd say, but there's no need to panic.
think: He could ride until about **2033** before needing to switch.
He'd want **a trade** anyway, because riding at 40 in the rain isn't a life.
do: Save for **two years**, then start the apprenticeship around 2029.
Share a flat with **Luis** to save £150 a month each.
feel: Pretty **calm**, apart from the usual **money worry**.
S4.quote: My knees already complain in the winter, so the robots just give me a date to get off the motorbike.
fieldNote: Pedro would leave riding **even without robots**, because of his knees.
He names **comfort** as the risk that could delay him.
Low costs and a clear plan bring him back to **uneasy**, close to his AI Plateau mood.

steps.text: Save for two years before starting the apprenticeship
Move in with Luis to cut rent by £150 a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to stop helping my mum to retrain, and I'd be training while still riding. What would help is apprenticeships that pay enough to live on, even at 28. Not a handout, just a fair wage while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about injuries. Everybody talks about robots taking delivery jobs, but my body will retire me before any robot does. Ask any rider over 35.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about robots taking delivery jobs, but my body will retire me before any robot does.
portrait: Pedro is **27**, rides a paid-off motorbike for FoodHop at night and lives alone above a launderette.
He sends his **mum £100** a month and has about three weeks saved.
He's **pragmatic**, using AI when it helps and waiting for proof before changing.
In every AGI picture he aims for an **electrician apprenticeship**; time only changes how hard it is.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to stop helping his mum while training and riding.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** that pay a fair wage to live on, even at 28.
